Abstract
Background: Neural radiance ﬁeld (NeRF) models have garnered signiﬁcant
attention for their impressive ability to synthesize high-quality novel scene views
from posed 2D images. Recently, the MedNeRF algorithm was developed to
render complete computed tomography (CT) projections from a single or a few
x-ray images further.Despite this advancement,MedNeRF struggles with accu-
rate pose reconstruction, crucial for radiologists during image analysis, leading
to blurry geometry in the generated outputs.
Purpose: Motivated by these challenges, our research aims to address Med-
NeRF’s limitations in pose accuracy and image clarity. Speciﬁcally, we seek to
improve the pose accuracy of reconstructed images and enhance the generated
output’s anatomical detail and quality.
Methods: We propose a novel pose-aware discriminator that estimates pose
differences between generated and real patches, ensuring accurate poses and
deeper anatomical structures in generated images. We enhance volumetric
rendering from single-view x-rays by introducing a customized distortion adap-
tive loss function and present the HTDataset, a new dataset pair that better
mimics machine-generated x-rays, offering clearer anatomical depictions with
reduced noise.
Results: Our method successfully renders images with correct poses and
high ﬁdelity, outperforming existing state-of-the-art methods. The results
demonstrate superior performance in both qualitative and quantitative metrics.
Conclusions: The proposed approach addresses the pose reconstruction chal-
lenge in MedNeRF, enhances the anatomical detail, and reduces noise in
generated images.The use of HTDataset and the innovative discriminator struc-
ture lead to signiﬁcant improvements in the accuracy and quality of the rendered
images, setting a new benchmark in the ﬁeld.

assess 3D information from a few x-ray images for
cost-effectiveness, but this relies heavily on human a

In the realm of imaging systems, initial methods
entailed creating mathematically compatible models to
gradually and analytically reconstruct the 3D details
of medical images.4 However, this approach encoun-
ters signiﬁcant limitations when the imaging system
is either unknown or incompatible with the estab-
lished mathematical model. With the emergence of
deep learning, there has been a notable shift towards
leveraging sparse views to reconstruct 3D CT data
from a limited set of 2D medical images.5–8 Although
these methods successfully address uncertainties in
imaging systems and discrepancies in mathematical
models, they necessitate annotated data and super-
vised paired 3D data. As a result, the substantial costs
associated with annotation and training pose challenges
to the widespread application of these techniques in
specialized medical domains.
The neural radiance ﬁelds (NeRF) model, introduced
in ref. [9], presents a novel approach for estimating
a 3D volumetric representation from images. It cap-
tures the radiance ﬁeld and density of the scene
using the parameters of a neural network. The neu-
ral network can generate new views through volume
rendering by sampling points along rays cast into the
scene. However, these representations are typically
obtained under controlled conditions,10 hence restricting
the direct application of NeRF in the medical ﬁeld.11
The generative neural radiance ﬁeld (GRAF)12 over-
comes some limitations of its predecessor NeRF by
addressing control settings and static scenes. However,
it fails to render overlapping anatomical structures in
medical imaging. Recent advanced method, such as
MedNeRF,11 have expanded the utilization of GRAF to
the medical domain by rendering CT projections with
minimal data, as few or even a single-view x-ray. Med-
NeRF has demonstrated the ability to generate realistic
images and provide a continuous representation of how
anatomical structures’ attenuation and volumetric depth
vary across different viewpoints without 3D supervision.
Despite its achievements, the model faces difﬁculties
in accurately reconstructing images in explicit poses,
which holds great signiﬁcance, particularly in medical
settings. This particular challenge further leads to the
generation of output with blurred geometry.
Motivated by the above challenges, we present our
method as an improving pose accuracy and geometry
in NeRF-based medical image synthesis,which extends
from MedNeRF.11 This improvement is made possible by
implementing a pose regularization branch in the dis-
criminator architecture. The pose regularization branch
facilitates the discriminator’s ability to distinguish if the
generated patch aligns accurately with the same pose
in the real patch. Consequently, this process compels
the generator to develop a heightened comprehension
of precise poses, signifying a distinct contribution to
our work.
Moreover, our work extends beyond pose regulariza-
tion and discriminator performance. We have improved
the process of volumetric rendering using single-view
x-ray images by incorporating a customized distortion
static adaptive loss function.This approach modiﬁes the
generation objective, resulting in a substantial enhance-
ment in image quality.This improvement is a noteworthy
addition to our research,highlighting the practical impact
of our work in image reconstruction and rendering.
Furthermore, it is worth noting that our discriminator
continues to consistently delivers a robust and compre-
hensive signal to the generator, especially when dealing
with CT scans.
Additionally, although MedNeRF11 datasets prove
to be useful for this task, it is undoubtedly clear
that the generated digitally reconstructed radiography
(DRR) images from the datasets lack clarity in depict-
ing anatomical structures and exhibit excessive noise,
thereby impacting the ﬁnal results. Therefore, we gen-
erate new pairs of datasets, that is, HTChest, HTKnee,
and HTHead (HTDataset) to address those challenges.
Conversely, our new HTDataset (see Figure 5) portrays
intricate anatomical details and demonstrates reduced
noise levels, thereby enhancing the ﬁnal results.
The main contribution of our work can be summarized
as follows:
1. The pose-aware discriminator was proposed to
enhance the discriminator pose estimation and
hence enforce the generator to learn the correct
poses.
2. The customized distortion static adaptive loss func-
tion is proposed and at the generation objective to
enhance an incentive balance between blurriness
and accuracy.
3. The new pair of datasets named HTDataset (HTCh-
est, HTKnee, and HTHead) that depicts intricate
anatomical structures and contains less noise,were
generated to overcome the challenges observed on
MedNeRF DRR dataset.
4. The proposed method achieves high-ﬁdelity ren-
dering with better image pose than other state-
of-the-arts (SOTAs) methods by adding a pose
regularization branch at the discriminator and dis-
tortion static adaptive loss function at the generation
objective.

RELATED WORKS
The representation of a scene in neural networks
encompasses various techniques, like occupancy or
signed distance functions for geometry and methods
encoding both appearance and geometry.13–20 Recent
advances leverage implicit neural representations with
multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs),21–24 with NeRF9 being
a notable method. NeRF models a scene as a vector-
valued function f(x, y, z, 𝜃, 𝜗) = (r, g, b, 𝜎), where (x, y, z)
are spatial coordinates, (𝜃, 𝜗) the viewing direction, and
(r, g, b, 𝜎) represent color and volume density. This func-
tion is used in volume rendering to generate new views.
However, NeRF requires large datasets of posed train-
ing images, which can be challenging in medical ﬁeld
where such data is scarce.
The impressive performance of NeRF has inspired
extensions like GRAF,12 which generates category-
speciﬁc radiance ﬁelds using shape and appearance
codes within a GAN framework, enabling unsupervised
training on unconstrained images without ground truth
camera poses. However, GRAF struggles with medical
data, such as DRR images, due to its inability to dif-
ferentiate anatomical structures from the background.11
To address this, MedNeRF11 adapts GRAF for medi-
cal applications, generating CT projections from few or
single-view x-rays without 3D supervision. Both mod-
els rely on a Gaussian distribution for pose estimation,
which can lead to faulty geometry and misaligned poses
if inaccurately estimated.
Moreover, on the task of volumetric rendering from
a single-view x-ray, MedNeRF modiﬁes the generation
objective by adding the distortion mean squared error
(MSE) loss function to incentivize a balance between
blurriness and accuracy. The averaging nature of MSE
poses difﬁculties in effective learning and representing
complex texture regions, leading to challenges in pre-
cisely capturing intricate signal structures. To address
these challenges,our model employs a pose regulariza-
tion branch at the discriminator to enforce the generator
to learn the correct pose. Moreover, we introduce the
customized distortion static adaptive ﬁlter to modify
the generation objective and improve the perceptual of
rendered reconstructed images.
Similar to our work25, found that training with only
adversarial loss can lead to sensitivity to random ini-
tialization, especially with certain objects, sometimes
resulting in convex objects appearing concave after
training. To address this, they added a camera pose
regularization branch to ensure accurate pose learn-
ing by comparing generated and real image poses.
Additionally,26 used a pose regularization branch to
tackle inaccurate pose estimation in natural images,
which can disrupt geometric learning. Their discrimi-
nator learns pose distributions under generator super-
vision using the 𝓁2 (Euclidean) function, though this
method is less robust to small image perturbations,27
highlighting a limitation compared to our model.

METHOD
In this work,we propose a new Medical 3D-aware image
synthesis paradigm to ensure the model pose accu-
racy and geometry. To achieve this goal, we modify the
generator and re-design the discriminator in conven-
tional 3D-aware GANs.11,12 Speciﬁcally, the pose-aware
discriminator extracts a pose from the given image
and uses it as the conditional label when performing
real/fake classiﬁcation. The summarized full framework
is shown in Figure 1 and detailed generator and discrim-
inator in Figures 2 and 3 respectively. Furthermore, we
propose the customized distortion adaptive loss function
and the introduction of the new HTDataset.

Pose-aware discriminator part

and density values for volumetric rendering as prox-

ing absorption and color representing tissue optical
properties, analogous to CT attenuation coefﬁcients or
Hounsﬁeld units, enabling interpretable reconstructions.
We enhance performance by introducing a novel pose
aware discriminator and a reﬁned training objective to
handle limited datasets and render deeper anatomical
structures as explained in details below. Additionally, we
propose a distortion adaptive loss function to balance
blurriness and accuracy in generation.
Pixel sampling:The sampled real patch P is obtained
by querying the image I at the 2D coordinates P(u, s)
using a bilinear interpolation function Γ(I, 𝜐). In order to
preserve high-frequency details, I was not downsam-
pled based on s, instead queried at speciﬁc spatial
locations.12

distributions in feature space, where a lower KID value

difference between the original and model-generated
images, emphasizing luminance accuracy, where SSIM
provides a comprehensive assessment of luminance,

3.8
Introduction to ablation study
The ablation studies aimed to evaluate the impact of
the discriminator pose regularization branch on the
overall system. In the ﬁrst experiment, to understand
the capability of the IMED loss function used in our
pose regularization branch,we replaced it with standard
Euclidean distance (L2NOM). Additionally, we incorpo-
rated the pose regularization branch into the original
GRAF12 framework and trained it as per its docu-
mentation. We presented more of the results on other
parameters in our supplementary material.
Succinctly, for all experiments, we choose the projec-
tion parameters (u, v) to evenly sample points on the
surface of a sphere, precisely a slight horizontal ele-
vation of 70-85◦and umin = 0, umax = 1 for a full 360◦
vertical rotation. Nonetheless, during training, we sup-
ply only one-ﬁfth of the views (72) views at intervals of
5◦, leaving the model to generate the remaining views
through rendering. For each experiment, the models
were trained for 200k iterations by using NVIDIA GTX
3090 with 24GB memory.

Abstract: Background: Neural radiance ﬁeld (NeRF) models have garnered signiﬁcant attention for their impressive ability to synthesize high-quality novel scene views from posed 2D images. Recently, the MedNeRF algorithm was developed to render complete computed tomography (CT) projections from a single or a few x-ray images further.Despite this advancement,MedNeRF struggles with accu- rate pose reconstruction, crucial for radiologists during image analysis, leading to blurry geometry in the generated outputs. Purpose: Motivated by these challenges, our research aims to address Med- NeRF’s limitations in pose accuracy and image clarity. Speciﬁcally, we seek to improve the pose accuracy of reconstructed images and enhance the generated output’s anatomical detail and quality. Methods: We propose a novel pose-aware discriminator that estimates pose differences between generated and real patches, ensuring accurate poses and deeper anatomical structures in generated images. We enhance volumetric rendering from single-view x-rays by introducing a customized distortion adap- tive loss function and present the HTDataset, a new dataset pair that better mimics machine-generated x-rays, offering clearer anatomical depictions with reduced noise. Results: Our method successfully renders images with correct poses and high ﬁdelity, outperforming existing state-of-the-art methods. The results demonstrate superior performance in both qualitative and quantitative metrics. Conclusions: The proposed approach addresses the pose reconstruction chal- lenge in MedNeRF, enhances the anatomical detail, and reduces noise in generated images.The use of HTDataset and the innovative discriminator struc- ture lead to signiﬁcant improvements in the accuracy and quality of the rendered images, setting a new benchmark in the ﬁeld.
